where: Section 1 (Hooke's law for tension and shear)
problem: The text says the law holds up to the elastic limit. Strictly, proportionality ends at the proportional limit, which lies at or below the elastic limit; between the proportional limit and the elastic limit the curve bends but unloading is still elastic. The same loose statement is repeated in the lead and in quiz Q1.
fix: Say: the straight line holds up to the proportional limit; unloading is fully elastic only up to the elastic limit, which is at or just above the proportional limit. Hooke's law is the linear part, not the whole elastic range.

where: Section 3, bullet on cost of failure
problem: "IRCTC bridge" is a wrong name. IRCTC is the railway catering and tourism corporation; it does not build bridges, so the example misleads a reader.
fix: Write "a railway bridge" (or "an Indian Railways bridge").

where: Section 3, bullet on loads being larger than estimated
problem: "A Chennai power cut that starts a pump against a closed valve" is physically confused. A power cut stops a pump; the surge comes when supply returns and the pump restarts against a closed valve.
fix: Write "a Chennai power cut whose restoration restarts a pump against a closed valve, giving a pressure surge".

problem: "Do not replace σ by P/(nA) and call it safe" does not say what P/(nA) is being compared with. Comparing P/(nA) with the working stress is conservative; the real error is comparing it with the failure stress (equivalently, P/n with σf A). A student can misread the trap.
fix: Write: never compare P/(nA) with the failure stress σf; that is the same as comparing P/n with σf A and it passes loads up to n times the safe load. Compare P/A with σw = σf/n, i.e. P ≤ σf A/n.
